newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria sends troops into troubled oil town.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria sends troops into troubled oil town.

text.p: Nigeria's military authorities said on Wednesday that soldiers had been sent into the troubled oil-producing town of Warri in the midwest to restore order.
Warri residents, reached by telephone from Lagos, said armed soldiers were patrolling the streets and manning key sites in the town.
"They are checking vehicles and people's bags for arms but they are not harrassing anyone," said one local journalist.
He said markets which had been shut for days were partially open and many people were venturing into the streets where gangs of armed youths had been in control.
The deployment of troops followed a recommendation by local military administrator Colonel John Dungs that the police could not cope with riots.
"The troops were sent in yesterday to complement the efforts of the police and their job is to help restore normalcy," defence headquarters spokesman Colonel Godwin Ugbo told Reuters.

Anarchy had reigned in Warri, 300 kms (190 miles) west of Lagos, since March 22 when clashes between armed youths broke out over the transfer of the local council headquarters from an Ijaw town to that of the rival Itsekiri tribe.
The death toll has risen to about 65 since April 12 when clashes resumed. A curfew imposed after the March clashes was lifted last week.

The independent Guardian newspaper reported on Wednesday the latest victims included a policeman while Punch, also independent, said a policeman had been kidnapped by rioters and several women abducted.
State radio reported the police began mass arrests of suspected rioters following the abductions.
"The presence of the military will restore confidence in civilians that they are being protected and forestall a complete breakdown of law and order," Ugbo said.

Royal Dutch Shell Group's Nigerian unit, which pumps roughly half Nigeria's oil output of about two million barrels per day (bpd), said it had closed one flow station and output was 2,000 bpd below normal.

At the height of the crisis in March, armed Ijaw tribesmen occupied six Shell oil flow stations, shutting off 100,000 bpd. A total of 127 of Shell's Nigerian staff held by the tribesmen were released after negotiations and oil output resumed.
A navy ship was sent to Warri last weekend to ensure that oil production, Nigeria's economic backbone, was not affected.
At the root of the crisis is a rivalry among three tribes -- the Ijaws, the Itsekiris and the Urhobos.
The Urhobos controlled affairs there in the 1970s until the Itsekiris, who provide the paramount ruler for Warri, began to press for more say in the town in the 1980s.
The Ijaws, who inhabit riverine areas, are the fourth largest tribe in Nigeria but are spread over six states where they are minorities except in the newly created Bayelsa state.
"Ijaw areas produce much of Nigeria's oil and their problem is far more serious than that of the Ogonis," said a senior Nigerian oil executive.
The Ogonis became famous in 1995 when minority rights campaigner Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogonis were hanged for the alleged murder of four pro-government Ogoni chiefs.
"The government must act quickly to end the Ijaw crisis otherwise oil production on shore will invariably be affected," said the oil executive.
